No slides were given for this lecture. The notes of Alessa, Alsalamah and Alomar word for word, in their own order (green), every gift (red) under the part it belongs to.

Notes

Topic Map

THREE IDEAS THAT ORGANIZE EVERYTHING

1 · LOCATION → COMPLICATION Aortic & visceral aneurysms rupture; limb (peripheral) aneurysms thrombose & embolize.·2 · LAPLACE DRIVES GROWTH ↑ radius × ↑ pressure → ↑ wall tension → more dilatation → rupture. Size & growth rate set the risk.·3 · WHEN TO REPAIR Intervene when expected rupture risk exceeds operative risk (elective open AAA repair ≈ 5% mortality).
Teal — fact / mechanism
Gold — rule of thumb / treatment
Red — danger / exception
EXAM flagged exam-important in the lecture
Notes

Definition & Classification

TermDefinition
AneurysmLocalized arterial dilatation ≥50% greater than the adjacent normal vessel diameter
ArteriomegalyDiffuse arterial enlargement — not a focal aneurysm
AAAAbdominal aortic diameter ≥3 cm
~1% general population aged >50·~8% high-risk: older adults, smokers, veterans

Overall prevalence ~1–8%. Less common in women and certain Asian/non-White populations — possibly smoking prevalence & genetics.

Notes

True vs False Aneurysm

FeatureTrue aneurysmFalse aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)
WallInvolves all 3 layers — intima, media, adventitiaWall disruption; the sac lacks the 3 arterial wall layers
MechanismDilatation of a weakened but intact wallBlood escapes through the defect into a contained sac
Typical causeDegenerative (most), genetic, inflammatory, infectiveTrauma or arterial puncture (e.g., femoral catheterization)
ShapeFusiform (circumferential) or saccular (one- sided outpouching)Sac connected to the artery by a neck
Telling apartMay look identical clinically → differentiate by imaging or intra-operative findings
Notes

Etiology

CauseMechanismKey associations & clues
Degenerative most commonWeakened elastic lamina & media; ↑ protease activity → collagen/elastin degradation, compounded by pulsatile pressure & altered hemodynamicsAccounts for most aneurysms
Genetic / connective tissueInherited structural defects of the arterial wallMarfan syndrome · Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Inflammatory non-infectiousLymphocyte & plasma-cell infiltration → protease release → wall destructionInflammatory disorders (e.g., arthritis) or adjacent inflammation (e.g., chronic pancreatitis); wall looks thickened & whitish
Infectious mycoticBacterial infection of the wall → inflammation & progressive wall destructionSalmonella (classic) · Brucella (Saudi Arabia — unpasteurized milk/dairy) · any artery, esp. the aorta · fever common
OtherCongenital/hereditary abnormalities · post-stenotic dilatation · post-dissection aneurysmal degeneration · trauma · iatrogenic arterial injury
MYCOTIC: CULTURES CAN MISLEAD
Blood cultures are frequently positive but may be negative → send tissue cultures from the surgical specimen.
MYCOTIC: TREATMENT
Excise/debride the infected segment + antibiotics + reconstruction — in-situ graft or extra-anatomic bypass (e.g., subcutaneous axillary-to-femoral) to keep graft material out of the infected field.
IATROGENIC
PSEUDOANEURYSM
Most commonly femoral after catheterization; radial access is lower-risk — superficial and easily compressed against bone.
Notes

Distribution & Natural History

ANATOMICAL DISTRIBUTION — MOST → LEAST COMMON

1 Infrarenal abdominal aorta Most common site; iliac involvement often accompanies AAA·2 Popliteal·3 Thoracic aorta·4 Femoral·5 Carotid & others other peripheral / visceral

MAIN COMPLICATION BY LOCATION

AORTIC · THORACIC · VISCERAL
RUPTURE
The feared, often fatal event → size thresholds drive repair
PERIPHERAL (LIMB) ANEURYSMS
THROMBOSIS &
EMBOLIZATION
Acute limb / digital ischemia; rupture is uncommon

vs

  • Most common site of abdominal aortic aneurysm → infrarenal aorta (answer recalled without the question). 435
Notes

Progression & Complications

Laplace's law: wall tension = pressure × radius. As radius or BP rises, tension rises → progressive dilatation, wall thinning and rupture risk.
Growth may be gradual (~1–2 mm/year) or irregular with periods of accelerated expansion → requires surveillance.
Altered/turbulent flow → mural thrombus → distal thromboembolization, particularly in peripheral aneurysms.
Enlargement can compress adjacent veins, nerves, organs and other structures — especially in confined anatomical spaces.
Notes

Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)

Risk Factors & Associated Aneurysms

Risk of developing AAA — the atherosclerotic profileFactors that raise rupture concern
• Advanced age and male sex
• Smoking — dose-dependent (cumulative pack-years)
• Hypertension
• Atherosclerotic / cardiovascular disease, incl. previous MI/CAD		• Larger diameter and rapid expansion
• Continued smoking and COPD
• Rising wall tension (Laplace)
• Female sex — rupture at smaller diameters
LOOK FOR THE PARTNER ANEURYSM EXAM
~50% of patients with a femoral/popliteal aneurysm have a concurrent AAA; peripheral aneurysms are less frequent among patients presenting with AAA. → In every AAA examine femoral & popliteal pulses; with any peripheral aneurysm, look for an AAA.
Notes

Clinical Presentation

Most are asymptomatic — increasingly detected incidentally with wider ultrasound/CT use.
Symptomatic, unruptured: persistent, deep abdominal or back pain (retroperitoneal) — generally not the belt-like radiation of pancreatic pain.
Large aneurysms may compress the duodenum, kidneys and ureters.
EXAMINATION IS INSENSITIVE
Fewer than 50% are diagnosed clinically; a palpable mass is more likely only with large aneurysms, and not every rupture shows the full triad.
  • The most common presentation of AAA → incidental finding. 437 ×4
  • A pulsating abdominal mass (in the acute setting) indicates → rupture of an AAA. 442
  • Incidental aneurysm managed conservatively → 4 cm. 439
Notes

Investigations

ModalityRoleStrengthsLimitations
UltrasoundScreening of choice; rapid bedside check in suspected ruptureInexpensive, readily available, no radiation, sensitive for dilatation; may show the aneurysm + associated fluidObesity and bowel gas reduce accuracy
CT / CTADiagnosis, anatomy & operative planningDiameter, shape, mural thrombus, normal proximal/distal vessels, branches, adjacent structures, renal anatomy, vascular anomaliesMeasure perpendicular to the centerline — oblique sections overestimate
Conventional angiographyMainly during interventionOutlines the patent, contrast-filled lumenUnderestimates size (mural thrombus not shown); not for primary diagnosis or diameter
Notes

Rupture Risk & Indications for Repair

REPAIR PRINCIPLE
Intervene when expected rupture risk exceeds operative risk — elective open repair mortality ≈ 5%, varying with comorbidities.
Rupture risk rises with diameter — progressively above 5 cm, particularly with continued growth.
Additional concerns: smoking, COPD, rapid enlargement and increasing wall tension.
SMALL & ASYMPTOMATIC → WATCH; DON'T EXPECT REVERSAL
Surveillance + cardiovascular risk-factor control. Medical treatment does not reverse established aneurysmal dilatation.

INDICATIONS FOR AAA REPAIR

DIAMETER ≥5.5 cm men ≥5.0 cm women Women rupture at smaller diameters·RAPID EXPANSION EXAM ≥0.5 cm in 6 mo ≥1 cm per year·SYMPTOMATIC Persistent abdominal/back pain, other abdominal causes excluded → Urgent repair after pre-op assessment & optimization·RUPTURED → Immediate emergency repair
Notes

Treatment: EVAR vs Open Repair

GOAL OF ANY REPAIR
Exclude the aneurysm sac from arterial pressure and blood flow → prevents further expansion, rupture and thromboembolic complications.
EVAR — endovascular aneurysm repairOpen surgical repair
HowStent-graft inside the aorta channels blood through the graft, not the sac. Main body + contralateral limb deployed & connected under fluoroscopy — demanding 3D positioning from 2D X-ray imagesReplace the aneurysmal segment with a sewn-in straight tube or bifurcated graft (5 steps below); transperitoneal or retroperitoneal approach
Anatomy neededSuitable proximal & distal landing zones (normal vessel above/below) for a secure seal & no endoleak; aortic neck shape, aneurysm anatomy, access vesselsNot dependent on landing zones
AdvantagesSmaller incisions, less blood loss, lower perioperative morbidity, shorter hospitalizationNo reliance on long-term imaging surveillance
DrawbacksGraft-related complications; long-term surveillance incl. annual CTHigher early morbidity; elective mortality ≈ 5%
ComplicationsGeneral: bleeding, infection, thrombosis Specific: endoleak (persistent flow into the sac), graft/limb occlusion, graft thrombosis, femoral access-site complicationsBleeding, infection, thrombosis · renal failure/ischemia · MI · lower-limb ischemia/limb loss · bowel/colonic ischemia · erectile dysfunction (sympathetic plexus near the bifurcation)

OPEN REPAIR IN FIVE STEPS

1 Clamp aorta above & below the aneurysm ›·2 Open the sac longitudinally·3 Control bleeding lumbar branches·4 Insert graft straight tube or bifurcated·5 Close sac over graft — shields adjacent organs
Notes

Ruptured AAA: Emergency Management

Sudden severe abdominal/back pain + hypotension/shock ± tender pulsatile mass. Not every patient shows the complete triad.·1 RECOGNIZE·ABCs · 2 large-bore IV lines Bloods, type & crossmatch Activate massive transfusion protocol Urgently notify vascular surgery/OR, anesthesia, ICU·2 RESUSCITATE & MOBILIZE·3 IMAGE·Unstable → bedside ultrasound for rapid assessment·Emergency open or endovascular repair·4 REPAIR
Stable → CTA, only if it won't delay definitive treatment
PERMISSIVE HYPOTENSION
Don't aggressively normalize BP before hemorrhage control: SBP ≈ 90 mmHg may be acceptable if perfusion is maintained — excessive BP elevation may worsen bleeding.
~50%
mortality even among those reaching care; many die pre-hospital, in ED, peri-op or in ICU (hemorrhage, age, CV disease)
  • Aorto-enteric fistula — the false statement → "always after surgery for AAA". 426
  • Size indicating surgery → 5.5 cm. 441
  • Pulsatile epigastric mass with BP 80/60 → keyed immediate laparotomy (straight to theatre — don't delay for CT). 430
Notes

Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA)

AAA VS TAA — WHO GETS IT & WHY

FeatureAAATAA
FrequencyMost common aneurysm (infrarenal aorta)Less common; rising with aging & more chest imaging
WhoOlder men; smokersOlder; greater male predominance; familial (first- degree relatives)
CausesDegenerative most commonDegenerative most common; post-dissection, connective tissue disorders, autoimmune/inflammatory, infection
Risk factorsAge, male, smoking (pack-years), HTN, CV diseaseSmoking, alcohol, age, HTN, COPD
Rupture risk ↑Diameter, growth, smoking, COPD, female sexDiameter, age, growth rate — ~1 cm/year is particularly concerning
Notes

Clinical Presentation

Structure compressedResult
EsophagusDysphagia
Trachea / airwaysRespiratory or irritation symptoms
Adjacent nervesNeurological / voice-related symptoms
Most asymptomatic — often discovered incidentally.
Pain: persistent chest, back or flank pain.
An enlarging aneurysm compresses neighboring structures (table).
  • Symptom distinguishing a thoracic from an abdominal aneurysm → cough and hoarseness (compression of the airway/recurrent laryngeal nerve). 441
Notes

Investigations & Treatment

TEVAR — THORACIC ENDOVASCULAR REPAIR
Stent-graft excludes the aneurysm from the circulation. Needs healthy proximal & distal landing zones and suitable access-vessel size. Less invasive, ↓ early morbidity. Open or hybrid open/endovascular repair when anatomy requires.
CT angiography = preferred imaging: size, anatomy, branches, surrounding structures, operative planning.
Ultrasound has a limited role (thoracic anatomy).
Conventional angiography: procedural planning/intervention, not initial diagnosis.
Repair at ~6 cm (lecture threshold), or if symptomatic, ruptured or rapidly expanding.
COMPLICATIONS OF THORACIC REPAIR
Stroke, spinal cord ischemia / paraplegia, major perioperative morbidity & mortality; long-term survival is limited by age & comorbidities.
Notes

Spinal Cord Ischemia

MECHANISM
Thoracic aortic branches contribute to spinal cord perfusion. Prolonged aortic coverage or interruption of these branches → spinal cord ischemia & paralysis; risk ↑ with extensive thoracic repair.
≈
−
↑ Arterial pressure — avoid hypotension; maintain or raise MAP to preserve spinal perfusion·SCPP spinal cord perfusion·↓ CSF pressure — CSF drainage lowers CSF pressure → widens the perfusion gradient·MAP keep it up ↑·CSF pressure drain it down ↓·Monitor post-op neurological function — especially lower-limb movement

AAA VS TAA — MANAGEMENT AT A GLANCE

FeatureAAATAA
ImagingUltrasound screens; CTA plansCTA (ultrasound limited by thoracic structures)
Repair≥5.5 cm men / ≥5.0 cm women; symptomatic; rupture; rapid growth~6 cm (higher morbidity of thoracic repair); symptomatic; rupture; rapid expansion
EndovascularEVARTEVAR (open or hybrid repair when anatomy requires)
Signature riskEndoleak (EVAR); bowel/renal ischemia, ED (open)Spinal cord ischemia / paraplegia, stroke
Notes

Peripheral Arterial Aneurysms

~70%
of peripheral aneurysms are popliteal
Most are initially asymptomatic.
Thrombosis & distal embolization are the major complications; rupture is relatively uncommon.
Enlargement → venous compression (→ DVT) and nerve compression (→ pain/neurological symptoms).

THE ISCHEMIC CASCADE

Turbulent flow in the dilated segment·Mural thrombus lines the sac·Thrombosis / embolization occlusion or distal emboli·Acute limb ischemia limb-threatening
WHY LIMB SALVAGE IS POOR
Thrombus is frequently chronic/organized → thrombectomy & thrombolysis work poorly → poor limb-salvage outcomes and substantial amputation risk.
Notes

Popliteal Aneurysms

WHEN TO REPAIR
Symptomatic: embolization, thrombosis, compression
Diameter ~2–2.5 cm, depending on patient/anatomical factors
Acute thrombosis/embolization → urgent/emergency intervention to prevent limb loss
HOW TO REPAIR
Preferred: surgical exclusion + autologous vein bypass (often a reversed vein graft)
Alternatives: prosthetic graft or endovascular stent-graft
PITFALLS
Stents suffer mechanical stress with knee/hip flexion → kinking, fracture or occlusion. Thrombolysis is often ineffective for large, chronic organized thrombus — not routinely preferred for longstanding aneurysm- associated thrombosis.
Notes

Femoral Aneurysms & Pseudoaneurysms

True femoral aneurysms are relatively uncommon; pseudoaneurysms are frequently iatrogenic after femoral catheterization.
Femoral > radial risk: deeper location, harder to compress, obesity.
Ultrasound-guided puncture reduces access complications and pseudoaneurysm formation.
Infected (mycotic) pseudoaneurysms in IV drug users after repeated arterial injection — venous thrombophlebitis/scarring drives them to alternative sites.
Complications: thrombosis/embolization · femoral nerve compression (pain/neuro) · venous compression (swelling/DVT).
Notes

Imaging of Peripheral Aneurysms

Duplex ultrasound
1st
Superficial, accessible vessels. Shows dimensions, flow, neck, thrombus and
true vs pseudoaneurysm
CTA / MRA + when more anatomical definition is needed·Arteriography Rx mainly during intervention — underestimates size (flowing lumen only)
Notes

Pseudoaneurysm Treatment

OptionHow it worksBest use / caution
US-guided compressionPressure over the neck → interrupts flow → sac thrombosisNon-invasive
US-guided thrombin injectionThrombin into the sac → induces clottingBest with a narrow, suitable neck
Surgical repairDirect open repairWhen percutaneous methods are unsuitable or complications require intervention
WIDE NECK = NO THROMBIN
With a wide neck, thrombin can enter the parent artery → arterial thrombosis/embolization.
Notes

Subclavian Artery Aneurysms

THORACIC OUTLET SYNDROME
Compression between the
first/cervical rib and scalene muscles — athletes or anatomical
abnormalities. Structures: subclavian artery, subclavian vein, brachial plexus.
Rare; usually true aneurysms; occasionally present as a tortuous artery or a pulsatile mass.
Causes: degenerative, post-stenotic dilatation, clavicular trauma/fracture, arterial thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS).
Post-stenotic dilatation: narrowing → turbulent flow & abnormal pressure distal to the stenosis → aneurysmal enlargement.

ARTERIAL TOS → ANEURYSM → EMBOLI

Rib / scalene compression repeated arterial narrowing ›·Post-stenotic dilatation subclavian aneurysm·Distal embolization recurrent small emboli·Digital ischemia finger pain, intermittent ischemia — sometimes over months
MAIN CONCERN
Distal embolization — not rupture.
TREATMENT
Aneurysm resection + surgical arterial reconstruction, or endovascular stent-graft in suitable anatomy.
Notes

Radial Artery Aneurysms

Usually pseudoaneurysms after arterial catheterization — much less common than femoral ones (superficial artery, compressed against bone).
Small caliber → more susceptible to post-puncture thrombosis.
The hand has a dual supply (radial + ulnar); the ulnar artery commonly provides the major collateral flow.
Reconstructing the small radial artery is technically difficult — and unnecessary if collateral circulation is sufficient.

IATROGENIC PSEUDOANEURYSM: FEMORAL VS RADIAL

FemoralRadial
FrequencyMost common iatrogenic siteMuch less common
WhyDeep, difficult to compress; obesitySuperficial, compressible against bone
Special issuesMycotic pseudoaneurysm in IV drug users; femoral nerve & venous compressionSmall caliber → thrombosis; hand relies on ulnar collateral
Prevention / RxUS-guided puncture; US compression, thrombin injection or surgeryAllen's test → ligate if collateral adequate, otherwise reconstruct
Notes

Visceral Artery Aneurysms

Relatively uncommon; most patients have a single aneurysm.

DISTRIBUTION

Splenic ~60%·Hepatic → others
Rupture is the principal feared complication — unlike peripheral

limb aneurysms, where thromboembolization predominates.

Splenic (most common) → hepatic → other visceral branches, including the superior mesenteric and renal arteries.

CLUE
Multiple visceral aneurysms → suspect underlying infection or vasculitis/inflammatory disease.
Notes

Splenic Artery Aneurysms

PREGNANCY — THE DANGER SCENARIO
Rupture concern rises markedly in pregnancy, especially the third trimester:
These risks drive treatment even when the aneurysm is otherwise small.
~75%
~90%
maternal mortality
fetal mortality
Most common visceral aneurysm; more frequent in women.
Associated with fibromuscular dysplasia (narrowing → post- stenotic dilatation).
Portal hypertension/liver disease also associated — partly because these patients are imaged more often.
Usually small, asymptomatic, incidental; spontaneous rupture relatively uncommon.
REPAIR INDICATIONS
Diameter >2 cm
Symptomatic
Woman of childbearing age (pregnancy rupture risk)
TREATMENT OPTIONS
Endovascular: coil embolization or covered stent when feasible
Surgical ligation/resection or reconstruction — by location & collateral circulation
Proximal/mid → reconstruction or exclusion without splenectomy · distal/hilar → may need splenectomy
  • Incidental AAA — indication for surgery → symptomatic (not 3.5–4 cm or hypertension). 437
Notes

Hepatic Artery Aneurysms

Less common than splenic; more frequent in men.
Rupture mortality ~35%; bleeding may occasionally be partially contained by surrounding structures.
Rupture into the biliary tree → hemobilia.
PATTERN TO RECOGNIZE
Abdominal pain + GI bleeding + jaundice = hemobilia → suspect a hepatic artery aneurysm bleeding into the biliary tree.
WHY LIGATION IS TOLERATED
The portal vein supplies most hepatic blood flow and carries oxygenated blood → partly supports the liver after arterial ligation.

TREATMENT

Surgical or endovascular, depending on aneurysm site & arterial anatomy.
Portal vein ~70–75%·Hepatic artery
Ligation possible when collateral hepatic perfusion is sufficient; some transient hepatic ischemia may follow.
Reconstruction if collaterals are inadequate or critical branches are involved.
Notes

Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) Aneurysms

TREATMENT
Surgical excision/ligation ± bypass/reconstruction, by location & importance of the branches:
Preserve or reconstruct major intestinal branches → prevents bowel ischemia
Distal branches may be ligated if collaterals suffice
Ischemic or involved bowel → segmental resection
Uncommon; a substantial proportion are mycotic/infectious.
May involve the main SMA trunk or its branches.
Presentation: abdominal pain; complications: rupture, bowel ischemia, involvement/fistulation into adjacent bowel.
Imaging: CT/CTA preferred — ultrasound limited by bowel gas.
INFECTION RULE
Avoid endovascular grafts/stents in active infection — risk of graft contamination/infection.
Added explanationAorto-enteric fistula — usually secondary (after aortic graft surgery, typically to the 3rd/4th duodenum) presenting with a "herald" GI bleed; primary fistulas (an untreated AAA eroding into bowel) also exist — so it is not "always" after surgery.
Notes

Renal Artery Aneurysms

Relatively uncommon; more frequent in women.
Frequently saccular, often near the first renal artery bifurcation.
Many idiopathic; associations: fibromuscular dysplasia, atherosclerosis, inflammatory arterial disease.

RENOVASCULAR HYPERTENSION

Most are asymptomatic/incidental.
Spontaneous rupture is rare, but pregnancy substantially increases concern.
CTA for anatomical assessment & surveillance.
Aneurysm disturbs or compresses renal arterial flow·↓ Renal perfusion ± branch ischemia·RAAS activation renin–angiotensin– aldosterone·Hypertension renovascular
REPAIR INDICATIONS
Diameter >2 cm
Women of childbearing age
Uncontrolled renovascular HTN
Symptomatic, or compromised renal perfusion/function
TREATMENT
Endovascular stent-graft or surgical reconstruction, by size, location & branch involvement. Repair may improve renal blood flow and reduce hypertension/antihypertensive needs. Aneurysms at complex branch points or near the hilum are difficult endovascularly → more complex reconstruction.

VISCERAL ANEURYSMS SIDE BY SIDE

Notes

Mastery Checklist

1 True vs false: a true aneurysm involves all 3 wall layers (fusiform or saccular); a pseudoaneurysm is a wall
breach with a contained sac (trauma/puncture) — tell them apart on imaging.
2 Site predicts the danger: aortic & visceral aneurysms → rupture; popliteal, femoral & subclavian →
thrombosis and distal embolization.
3 Laplace: ↑ radius × ↑ pressure → ↑ wall tension → growth → rupture. Typical growth ~1–2 mm/year, but it
can accelerate → surveillance.
4 AAA repair: ≥5.5 cm men / ≥5.0 cm women, symptomatic (urgent), ruptured (immediate), or rapid growth
≥0.5 cm in 6 months or ≥1 cm/year. Medical therapy does not reverse dilatation.
5 Partner aneurysms: ~50% of femoral/popliteal aneurysm patients have an AAA → examine femoral &
popliteal pulses in every AAA, and look for an AAA with any peripheral aneurysm.
6 Ruptured AAA: pain + shock + pulsatile mass, but the triad is often incomplete and exam misses >50%.
Unstable → bedside US; stable → CTA only if no delay. Permissive hypotension (SBP ≈ 90 mmHg); mortality ~50%.
7 Imaging traps: US screens (obesity/bowel gas limit it); CTA plans — measure perpendicular to the centerline;
angiography sees only the lumen → underestimates.
8 EVAR vs open: EVAR needs landing zones, has lower early morbidity, but carries endoleak risk + annual CT;
open repair ≈ 5% mortality with renal/bowel ischemia, MI and erectile dysfunction.
9 TAA: CTA, repair ~6 cm. Spinal cord ischemia: SCPP ≈ MAP − CSF pressure → avoid hypotension, drain
CSF, watch lower-limb movement.
10 Popliteal: ~70% of peripheral aneurysms; repair ~2–2.5 cm or symptomatic; autologous (reversed) vein
bypass preferred; stents kink across the knee; thrombolysis fails on organized thrombus.
11 Pseudoaneurysms: femoral ≫ radial (deep vs superficial). Treat with US-guided compression or thrombin
(narrow neck only). Radial → Allen's test → ligate if ulnar collateral adequate.
12 Mycotic: Salmonella classic, Brucella in Saudi Arabia (raw dairy); blood cultures may be negative → tissue
culture. Excise/debride + antibiotics + in-situ or extra-anatomic bypass; no endografts in active infection (e.g., SMA).
13 Visceral: splenic ~60% (women, FMD; repair >2 cm/symptomatic/childbearing age; pregnancy rupture
~75% maternal, ~90% fetal mortality) · hepatic (men; hemobilia = pain + GI bleed + jaundice) · renal (>2 cm; renovascular HTN via RAAS).
